\textbf{Single-task results.} We fine-tune a separate policy for each HumanoidArena task, comparing two initialization strategies. Kimodo-Policy is fine-tuned directly on task data, whereas Kimodo-Policy$^{*}$ initializes ControlNet and the hand head from our 419-hour VLA policy-pretraining stage. RTC is disabled for both variants to match the reported baselines. Kimodo-Policy achieves the highest overall success rate (SR; 69.51\%), exceeding DP~\cite{chi2023diffusionpolicy}, the strongest baseline (60.0\%), by 9.51 percentage points. It also attains the lowest average fall rate (AFR; 4.29\%, tied with Kimodo-Policy$^{*}$) and highest average SR on human--scene interaction (HSI; 84.58\%). Kimodo-Policy$^{*}$ achieves 67.14\% overall SR and 84.17\% HSI SR, with the highest task-level SRs on OpenDoor (93.3\%) and VisNavi (76.7\%). The framework supports language-conditioned whole-body control: VLA pretraining improves selected tasks, whereas direct fine-tuning yields higher overall SR.

\textbf{Multi-task results.} We jointly train one policy on all seven HumanoidArena tasks and evaluate it in the SONIC-based setting~\cite{humanoidarena,sonic}, with RTC disabled to match the baseline protocol. In Table~\ref{tab:arena_multi_task}, Kimodo-Policy$^{*}$ achieves 72.14\% overall SR, exceeding the strongest baseline, $\pi_{0.5}$~\cite{pi05} (53.8\%), by 18.33 percentage points, with the lowest AFR (4.29\%). It attains the highest mean SRs for human--object interaction (HOI; 56.11\%) and human--scene interaction (HSI; 84.17\%), and leads on P\&Pbox (90.0\%), OpenDoor (95.0\%), SitSofa (96.7\%, tied), and VisNavi (76.7\%). Without VLA pretraining, Kimodo-Policy obtains 67.63\% overall SR and 51.67\% HOI SR, a decrease of only 1.88 percentage points in overall SR relative to single-task training. Thus, one shared policy can retain much of the task-specific performance across seven skills, with high success and low fall rates.

\textbf{Attention map analysis.} Figure~\ref{fig:attention} illustrates how Kimodo-Policy's visual focus varies with the task. Its attention is concentrated around task-defining objects and interaction regions, such as the ball in Football, the box in P\&P Box, and the punching bag in Boxing, while shifting to relevant scene elements for door opening, sitting, and navigation. By comparison, $\pi_{0.5}$ shows less localized responses to task-relevant regions, whereas Diffusion Policy distributes activation more broadly across the scene. This task-dependent pattern suggests that Kimodo-Policy's visual processing aligns with the semantics of the language instruction, emphasizing cues relevant to the current objective and supporting task-grounded action selection in the shared multi-task setting.
